clue.text: Lake circled by hungry tailless bird

indicators.note: circled by means surrounded, so the shortened word goes round the letter for lake
tailless means the last letter is cut off

parts.note: eager can mean keen or hungry for something
L is the standard map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A lake is ringed by a ravenous bird that has lost its tail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tailless bird' reads as one phrase, but 'tailless' works on the word for hungry, trimming EAGER to EAGE, while bird alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The eagle is a large bird of prey, so it is one example of a bird.

clue.text: Cross with journalists after European editor spoke

indicators.note: coming after something means following it, so the pieces line up in that order

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for European
a cross is drawn as X
the press is journalists collectively
ED is the abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: An angry editor from Europe addressed the reporters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like angry, describing someone's mood, but it is the letter X. 'After European' places the E ahead of the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: To express an opinion is to put it into words, so expressed can stand in for spoke.

clue.text: Good arguments for sprouts

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for good
a row is a noisy quarrel

explanation.surface: Sound reasons to eat Brussels sprouts, the vegetable many hate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sprouts' sounds like the vegetable, but it is a verb, and ROWS here rhymes with cows.
explanation.definitionFit: When a plant sprouts it puts out shoots and increases in size, which is what it does as it grows.

clue.text: Plain I've got over depression

indicators.note: something got over is flipped, and in a down clue it also sits on top

parts.note: taken as written, without the apostrophe
a dent is a hollow pressed into a surface

explanation.surface: A plain confession of having recovered from a bout of depression.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depression' suggests low mood; it is a physical hollow. The surface 'got over' means recovered, but it signals the turn.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain can mean obvious, clear to see, which is also what evident means.

clue.text: Feeling wicked, cutting off nearly everyone

indicators.note: to cut something off is to sever and remove it, so one piece is taken away from the end of the longer word
nearly means not quite all of it, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: wicked is slang for excellent or terrific

explanation.surface: A sense of evil in someone who snubs almost everybody they know.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wicked' looks like evil, but it is the slang of approval: wicked, sensational. Remove AL from its end and the noun is left.
explanation.definitionFit: A sensation is a physical perception, such as warmth or tingling, which is a feeling in the body.

clue.text: Dirk could be inside this studio initially with Ted?

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word is used

parts.note: the first letter of this word
Ted Heath was British Prime Minister from 1970 to 1974

explanation.surface: Could actor Dirk be in the studio alongside Ted, a celebrity get-together?
explanation.walkthrough: Dirk reads as a man's name (the actor Dirk Bogarde) paired with Ted, but a dirk is a Scottish dagger; Ted is Edward Heath, the Conservative prime minister.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheath is the close-fitting case a dagger or knife blade slides into for carrying.

clue.text: Supply iron and get new gas

indicators.note: read as the adverb of supple, it means flexibly, so the letters bend into another order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: An instruction to a supplier: deliver iron and buy fresh gas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' looks like a verb meaning provide, but it is the adverb 'supple-ly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Nitrogen is the colourless gas that makes up most of the air, an example of a gas.

clue.text: Apart from oars, ignore the odd parts below

indicators.note: skipping the odd-numbered letters leaves only the even ones

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of this word
under is a synonym of below

explanation.surface: Advice to a rower about bits of the boat below, apart from the oars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apart from' reads as one phrase meaning except; it splits into the definition and a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Asunder is an old word meaning into pieces or separated, as in torn apart.

clue.text: Negotiate most of recent diet changes

indicators.note: changes means the letters are altered into a new arrangement
most of means all but the last letter of recent

explanation.surface: Someone is told to negotiate over the bulk of their latest diet changes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'most of' trims recent to RECEN, which joins diet as one pool of letters for 'changes' to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To intercede is to step in on another's behalf, mediating or negotiating between parties.

clue.text: Like an anorak on Debra — dry on a regular basis

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: An anorak on a woman named Debra stays dry when she wears it regularly.
explanation.walkthrough: An anorak is a waterproof jacket, which fits 'dry', but in British slang an anorak is an obsessive enthusiast with dull hobbies.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang calls an obsessive, socially awkward hobbyist an anorak, so behaving like one is being geeky.

clue.text: Leading dance in hospital department

parts.note: a prom is a formal school dance
taken as written
ENT is the ear, nose and throat department

explanation.surface: Someone is leading a dance in a hospital ward, perhaps at a staff party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container signal putting the dance inside the department, but it is simply the letters IN in the chain.
explanation.definitionFit: A prominent or leading figure is important and stands out among peers in the field.

clue.text: Perfect golf club softly scratched

indicators.note: a runner that is scratched is withdrawn from the race, so a letter is taken out

parts.note: the putter is the club used on the green
p (piano) is the musical marking for softly

explanation.surface: A flawless golf club gets gently scratched, spoiling its finish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scratched' pictures a mark on the club, but it means withdrawn, as a horse is scratched from a race, so the P of softly leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: Perfect can mean complete or absolute, as in a perfect stranger, which is also an utter stranger.

clue.text: English seat is possibly most comfortable

parts.note: E is the standard abbreviation for English

indicators.note: possibly suggests one of several arrangements, so the letters may be put in another order

parts.note: these two words supply the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A claim that an English chair may well be the comfiest one going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seat' seems to belong with 'comfortable', but it is only fodder for the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Easy can mean relaxed and free of discomfort, so the easiest position is the most comfortable one.

clue.text: Well-behaved soldier

definitions.meaning: first meaning: calm, tidy and disciplined
second meaning: a soldier who carries orders or attends an officer

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as praise for a soldier, but the two words are separate meanings of one word, one an adjective and one a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes neat, disciplined conduct, and the noun names an army attendant who does an officer's errands.

clue.text: In report, mentions tourist attractions

indicators.note: a report is something spoken and heard, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: to cite something is to mention it

explanation.surface: A newspaper report names the places tourists flock to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In report' seems to set the scene of a written article; it means spoken aloud, where CITES and the answer sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: The sights of a city are its famous landmarks and buildings that visitors go out to see.

clue.text: Christian maybe willing to receive the setter's news

indicators.note: whatever receives something takes it in, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: game means willing, as in game for anything
the setter is I, and 'the setter has' is I'VE
news read as plural of new, whose abbreviation N is doubled, as pages gives pp

explanation.surface: A Christian, maybe, is willing to hear the setter's latest news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Christian' suggests a believer; it is a Christian name. The setter's 'I've' and the doubled N go inside GAME after its G.
explanation.definitionFit: A Christian name is the first name given at baptism, an example of a personal first name.

clue.text: Gathers information from Edward about underwear

indicators.note: about can mean turned around, as in about-turn, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: Ed is the short form of Edward
briefs are close-fitting underpants

explanation.surface: Someone is quizzing Edward about his underwear, a comic scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' reads as 'on the subject of', but it turns ED round before the underwear is added.
explanation.definitionFit: To debrief someone is to question them after a mission or task to collect what they learned.

clue.text: It's of benefit if you have a flat belly

definitions.text: It's of benefit if you have a flat belly

parts.words: It's of benefit if you have a flat belly
parts.note: surface reading: praise for a toned stomach; setter's reading: a punctured tyre on a car, which calls for a replacement

explanation.walkthrough: The answer means two things: the extra wheel carried for a puncture, and slang for a roll of fat round the waist, the opposite of a flat belly.
explanation.definitionFit: A reserve wheel helps when a car has a flat, and the same phrase names a paunch of belly fat.

clue.text: Dreadful leaders in House of Representatives make fun of the French

indicators.note: leaders are the ones at the front, so the first letter of each word is used

parts.note: the first letters of the three words
to rib someone is to tease them
le is French for the

explanation.surface: Awful American congressmen mock the French, a political jibe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaders' suggests politicians running the House, but it asks for the initial letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Dreadful and horrible are near synonyms, both meaning very bad or unpleasant.

clue.text: Class conflict

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a category or grade, as a football league has tiers
second meaning: disagreement that splits people apart

explanation.walkthrough: 'Class conflict' reads as the political phrase about social classes, but the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A division is a grouping or tier in a ranking, and also a split or discord between people.

clue.text: Boss went missing with trainee

parts.note: a boss is also a round stud or knob on a surface

indicators.note: something missing is absent, so that letter is left out

parts.note: taken as written
W is the abbreviation for with

explanation.surface: The manager disappeared with a new recruit, a workplace scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boss' pictures a manager, but it is a raised knob, like a stud on a shield. 'Went missing with' reads as eloping; it removes W from WENT.
explanation.definitionFit: A trainee is someone learning a trade or skill, which is what a student is.

clue.text: Snaps out of it?

parts.note: surface reading: someone recovering from a bad mood; setter's reading: photographs, which come out of a certain device

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'snaps out of it' is an idiom for pulling yourself together; read literally, it describes snapshots emerging from an object.
explanation.definitionFit: Snaps is informal for photographs, and photographs are produced by the device that takes pictures.

clue.text: Article promises no advanced solutions

parts.note: an is the indefinite article

indicators.note: no means none of it, so that letter is taken away

parts.note: to swear is to promise solemnly
A is the abbreviation for advanced

explanation.surface: A magazine piece promises no sophisticated fixes, only simple ones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No advanced' seems to describe the solutions; it takes A out of SWEARS.
explanation.definitionFit: The solutions to a puzzle, such as this crossword, are its answers, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Ways England cricketer's caught

indicators.note: to catch words is to hear them, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: Joe Root is an England batsman and former captain, so Root's

explanation.surface: A cricket report on the manner in which an England player got out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught' pictures a catch dismissing the batsman; it means heard. The answer sounds like ROOTS in British speech, where it rhymes with boots.
explanation.definitionFit: A route is a way or path taken from one place to another.

clue.text: Best cur one trained? Without question

indicators.note: without can mean outside, so these letters go around another piece
something trained has been shaped and schooled into a new form, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: these two words supply the letters to rearrange
Q is the standard abbreviation for question

explanation.surface: Is a trained mongrel the finest dog? Beyond doubt, says a proud owner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Best' looks like an adjective praising the dog, but it is a verb meaning to beat. 'Without' is the old sense of outside, not lacking.
explanation.definitionFit: To best an opponent is to beat or overcome them, which is what conquering means.

clue.text: Hold cold fish

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap
the ling is a long cod-like sea fish

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hold cold fish' reads as keeping something chilled; hold is the verb that defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To cling to something is to grip or hold it tightly.

clue.text: Watch old boy work in the military

parts.note: OB is the abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil of a school
to serve is to be a member of the armed forces

explanation.surface: A former pupil is told to keep an eye on things while doing army duty.
explanation.walkthrough: An old boy is a British term for a former pupil of a school.
explanation.definitionFit: To observe something is to look at it attentively, a plain synonym of watch as a verb.

clue.text: Some stuck up colonel fires gun

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuck up' reads as snooty, describing the colonel, but in a down entry it means the letters run upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A rifle is a long-barrelled firearm, a kind of gun.

clue.text: Picture this writer's anger after finally getting dismissed

explanation.walkthrough: 'After' looks like a time word placing one piece behind another; here it is the word whose last letter, R, leaves RAGE.
explanation.definitionFit: An image is a picture or likeness, whether a photograph, painting or one in the mind.

clue.text: Stroke goat, perhaps, then step on it

explanation.definitionFit: Butterfly is a swimming stroke in which both arms sweep over together with a dolphin kick.

clue.text: Harry near guests lacking upper-class grandeur

clue.text: Vegetable marrows we'd eaten, though not all

parts.note: the run of letters spanning the three words

explanation.surface: The marrows had been eaten, though some were left over.
